newsitem.title: FRANCE: French doctors to stay on strike, seek gvt talks.
newsitem.headline: French doctors to stay on strike, seek gvt talks.

text.p: French junior hospital doctors protesting against government plans to cap health spending voted on Saturday to remain out on strike but left the door open for more negotiations.
A union representative said the vote was held among delegates from 23 of France's 26 teaching hospitals after a six-hour meeting in Paris and it supported an unlimited strike.
The strikers also called for a demonstration in the capital on April 13 and said they would resume surprise disruptions such as blocking roads and railways.
The doctors said they were waiting for a gesture from the government and were ready to meet with Social Affairs Minister Jacques Barrot to seek a resolution to the conflict.

Dragging into its fourth week, the movement has developed into a test of conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe's resolve to cut public deficits to allow France to qualify for the European Union's planned single currency in 1999.
The junior doctors want the government to scrap or delay plans to fine all doctors in a region, regardless of individual practice, if the area overshoots pre-set spending limits.
While the government has refused these demands and accused the strikers of promoting their own sectional interests, Barrot has offered to make the fines more individualised.
The strikers rejected the conciliatory step and stormed out of talks with Barrot after only 10 minutes on Friday, saying he was not offering them concrete proposals.
There are signs the movement may be losing momentum as the junior doctors, paid by the shift, begin to feel the pinch of the lengthy strike.

The daily newspaper Le Monde reported on Saturday that three teaching hospitals had abandoned the movement. Another newspaper, Liberation, reported that chief residents in 13 of the hospitals had gone back to work.
The junior doctors are supported by unions representing specialists in private practice, who have opposed the reforms from the time they were announced in late 1995.
